Assume small-deformation, linear-elastic behavior with an isotropic, homogeneous material (Young's modulus E, Poisson's ratio ν).
Model the beam as a slender prismatic member with a rectangular cross-section of width b and height h, so Euler-Bernoulli beam theory applies (length much greater than cross-section dimensions).
Assume pure bending (or bending where shear effects on stress are negligible at the fibers of interest), so plane sections remain plane and stress varies linearly through the depth.
Take the beam axis along x, the depth direction along y measured from the neutral axis at the centroid, and bending about the z principal axis.
Define the area moment of inertia about the bending axis as I = b·h³/12.
Write the bending moment distribution M(x) as a known function obtained from statics of the given loading and support conditions.
Compute the bending stress at an arbitrary fiber location y (measured from the neutral axis) using σ_x(y, x) = −M(x)·y / I, with the sign convention that positive M produces compression at fibers above the neutral axis (y > 0) and tension below.
Report the maximum stresses at the extreme fibers y = ±h/2: σ_max = ±M·(h/2)/I = ±6M/(b·h²).
Optionally compute curvature κ = M/(E·I) and the deflection w(x) from E·I·w''(x) = M(x) if bending response beyond stress is needed.
Validate results by checking that the neutral axis passes through the centroid, that stress is zero at y = 0, that stress is linear in y and independent of b except through I, and that extreme-fiber stresses are equal and opposite.
If numerical values or specific support/loading configurations are supplied later, substitute them into M(x) and the stress formula without changing the governing relations.
